title: Can one paper strip give both a third and a sixth?
description: A paper strip one unit long is folded into three equal parts to make one third. The folded strip is then folded in half, so each third is cut into two equal parts, and the new parts are named.
teaching_notes: One idea: folding the strip that is already folded into thirds cuts every third into two equal parts, so the parts get smaller and there are more of them. Watch for students who fold only the middle third.

source: Make 1/3 using a paper strip. Can you use this to also make 1/6?
video_script.why: The child folds a one unit strip into three equal parts, then folds the folded strip in half, and names the new parts by counting how many fit in the whole strip.
video_script.substitution: Fold the strip the way it was folded into two and then four equal parts, but start with three equal parts.
video_script.anchor: A paper strip one unit long, folded into three equal parts and then folded in half
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, folding the strip in half again gives one sixth

final_answer.value: Yes; 3 x 2 = 6 equal parts, each 1/6 unit
final_answer.spoken: yes, there are six equal parts, and each part is one sixth of a unit

never_show: 1/6 or 6 equal parts before the answer beat
maths_rules: the strip is 1 unit long; folding it into 3 equal parts makes each part 1/3 unit
keeping the folded strip folded and folding it in half creases every one of the 3 parts in the middle
each third is cut into 2 equal parts: 3 x 2 = 6 equal parts
1 unit shared into 6 equal parts: each part is 1/6 unit
check: the new parts are all equal and fill the whole strip
video_script.design: One idea: fold the strip again to cut each part into two. Same method as folding into halves and then fourths. The strip stays on the board to the end.
